name: Ben Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of six at Tallyho Media, in a unit behind the retail park, and we do ads for car dealerships, gyms and a chain of garden centres. A normal day is maybe forty versions of the same ad: a square one for social, a tall one for stories, a banner, a flyer, each with a different price. I start with an AI tool for rough layouts and captions, then I fix what it gets wrong, which is usually the hands and the small print. What wears me out is dealers ringing at five to change the finance offer on every single size.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of that uses AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, from the first coffee. Gina, who owns Tallyho, gave me the job of testing new tools because I kept showing her things on my phone. I'm not the best pure designer in the building, Hana is, but I'm the fastest at turning one idea into forty sizes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I've always said it's a good tool and not a miracle. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd post the odd before-and-after, because people like those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means life carries on and I've got a slight edge. The routine resizing it does is the part I already hand to it. My pay's normal and I've got about three months saved. If AI stays this small, I'm still the fastest designer at Tallyho Media, and car dealers always need ads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep selling the ad templates I put up online, which bring in maybe sixty a month. I'd ask Gina for a small raise next spring on the back of speed. And I'd keep saving, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. A bit bored at the thought of nothing changing, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Car dealers getting squeezed, maybe. If people stop buying cars on finance, the dealers cut their ad spend and Tallyho feels it. But that's normal business stuff, not something I lie awake over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays this small, what's your next move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably push the template thing harder, make it a hundred and fifty a month. It's fun and it's mine. I'd still want the agency job for the steady money though.

say: AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle, which is what I've always said.
I'd keep showing colleagues **shortcuts** and post the odd before-and-after online.
think: Life carries on and I keep a **slight edge** from being fast with the tools.
The **routine resizing** it takes over is work I already hand to it.
do: Keep selling **ad templates** online, which bring in about sixty a month.
Ask Gina for a **small raise** next spring based on my speed.
Keep saving steadily on top of the **three months** I have.
feel: **Fine**, and a little **bored** at the thought of nothing changing.
S0.quote: If AI stays this small, I'm still the fastest designer at Tallyho Media, and car dealers always need ads.
fieldNote: He sees his value as **speed and tools**, not raw design talent, and says so openly.
His only real worry here is **car dealers** cutting ad budgets, which he treats as normal business.
The **template side income** matters to him more as something of his own than for money.

steps.text: Keep building dealership ads with AI rough layouts first
Grow online ad template sales to 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for designers who learn the tools, and the ones who don't will struggle. At work I'd volunteer to train everyone. Online I'd probably start a small channel showing real agency workflows, because nobody shows the boring honest version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Tallyho hires fewer people and I'm one of the ones who stays, because I'm the one making the tools work. But the agency probably doesn't replace Hana or the junior when they leave. That's not my job going, but it's the office getting smaller around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gina to make me the production lead, officially, with a raise, since I'd be running the tools. I'd learn the automation side properly, the stuff that pulls prices from a dealer's stock list and builds every ad size in one go. And I'd put two hundred a month extra into savings, just in case I'm wrong about being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, a bit guilty. I'm fine, but I'm watching people around me get nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Tallyho would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana's a lovely illustrator, properly talented, and she hates the tools. I'd try to help her, but you can't make someone learn. If she left, I'd feel like I'd built the thing that pushed her out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be building the very tools that make the office smaller. Does that sit oddly with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. Wanting to stay safe and wanting to build the AI tools are the same thing for me. I'd rather hold the steering wheel than stand in the road.

say: This is the moment for designers who **learn the tools**; those who don't will struggle.
I'd start a small channel showing **honest agency workflows** and train colleagues.
think: Tallyho hires **fewer people**, and I'm likely one who stays because I run the tools.
Hana and the junior **won't be replaced** when they leave, so the office shrinks around me.
do: Ask Gina for an official **production lead** role with a raise.
Learn the **automation** that builds every ad size from a dealer's stock list.
Put an extra **two hundred a month** into savings in case I'm wrong.
feel: **Interested** and a little **guilty**, watching colleagues grow nervous.
S1.quote: Wanting to stay safe and wanting to build the AI tools are the same thing for me. I'd rather hold the steering wheel than stand in the road.
fieldNote: He expects his **own job** to survive while the agency shrinks around him.
Real **guilt about Hana**, a talented illustrator who refuses the tools.
His public message is upbeat; privately he hedges with **extra savings**.

steps.text: Ask Gina for the production lead title and a raise
Set up automatic ad sizing from dealers' stock lists
Save an extra 200 a month for a year
Start a small channel showing real agency workflows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: if it can do any thinking work, it can do mine, so let's not pretend. At work I'd tell Gina we've got about a year to work out what Tallyho even is. Online I'd say people should save hard and learn something physical as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my edge is speed with the tools, and in this world the tools don't need me. A car dealer would just ask the AI for forty ad sizes and get them. I'd give myself maybe a year of useful work before the job's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd squeeze everything into savings, cancel the gym and the car lease, and get to six months. I'd try to make money fast from the knowledge while it's still worth something, like setting up AI ad systems for other small agencies. And I'd look at hands-on work that buys three years, like fitting large-format prints and vehicle wraps, because the robots come around 2031 in this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one, but two years is brutal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell your knowledge. For how long is that worth anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said, it's mostly one year of being the guy who knows how to set it up. After that the AI can set itself up. So I'd charge for that year properly and not do favours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ring first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call Petra, my sister, who runs a print shop with her husband. I'd ask if they'd train me on wrap fitting and give me some shifts. I'd feel a bit silly, being the tech guy asking my sister Petra to teach me to use a squeegee.

say: If AI can do **any thinking work**, it can do mine, so let's not pretend.
People should **save hard** and learn something **physical** as a backup.
think: My edge is **speed with tools**, and in this world the tools don't need me.
I'd give myself about **one year** of useful work before the job is gone.
do: Cancel the **gym and car lease** and push savings to six months.
Sell **AI ad setups** to other small agencies while that knowledge pays.
Ask my sister Petra for **wrap-fitting** training and shifts at her print shop.
feel: **Alarmed**, which is unusual for him; two years feels brutal.
S2.quote: I'd feel a bit silly, being the tech guy asking my sister Petra to teach me to use a squeegee.
fieldNote: The adaptive early adopter sees his **advantage vanish** fastest in this version.
He turns at once to **cash in the knowledge** for a year, then moves to hands-on work.
Family, through his sister's **print shop**, is his bridge, not government help.

steps.text: Push savings to six months of costs this year
Cancel the gym membership and hand back the car lease
Set up AI ad systems for other small agencies, paid
Train on vehicle wrap fitting at Petra's print shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something smart, if you start now. At work I'd push Gina to turn Tallyho into the agency that runs the AI for small businesses. Online I'd talk about it openly, with real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think there's a three or four year window where people like me are worth a lot, and then not. Wages for graphic design won't survive 2031, so the trick is owning something by the end, a client list or a share of a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask Gina for a small share in Tallyho in exchange for building the AI side. I'd set up a proper business for my templates and setups. I'd keep at least four months saved, and by year three I'd learn wrap and signage fitting at Petra's shop at weekends, so there's a hands-on string for 2031 to 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. It's the kind of worry that gets you out of bed early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Gina says no to a share?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go out on my own sooner. There are enough dealers who know me. I'd rather take the risk than be the last designer at an agency in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to people like you after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe the people who own the clients do fine for a while, and everyone else doesn't. I'd want to be on the right side of that, but I can't promise I will be.

say: Five years is enough to do **something smart**, if you start now.
Tallyho should become the agency that **runs AI** for small businesses.
think: There's a **short window** where my skills pay well, then they don't.
Owning a **client list or share** matters, because design wages won't survive 2031.
do: Ask Gina for a **share in Tallyho** in return for building the AI side.
Set up a **proper business** for templates and AI setups.
Learn **wrap and signage fitting** at weekends from year three.
feel: **Anxious** in a busy way, the kind of worry that gets him up early.
S3.quote: Wages for graphic design won't survive 2031, so the trick is owning something by the end, a client list or a share of a business.
fieldNote: He reframes the problem as **owning versus earning**: client lists and shares, not salary.
He'd **leave Gina** and go solo rather than be the last designer standing.
Honest that he **can't promise** he lands on the right side.

steps.text: Ask Gina for a share of Tallyho for building the AI side
Register a small business for templates and AI ad setups
Learn wrap and signage fitting at Petra's shop at weekends
Keep at least four months of costs saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we actually get to plan, so plan. At work I'd still be pushing the tools. Online I'd be the annoying guy telling everyone to start a side business now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty good about it. Ten years is long enough to build something real, and I'd be 37 at the end with, hopefully, a small business that owns its clients. The graphic design job still goes in ten years, but I'd have moved before it did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Tallyho for two or three years, get the production lead role, and learn everything about how dealers buy ads. Then I'd go out on my own with a few of them, running their ads with AI, charging a monthly fee. I'd put money into a simple index fund every month, and I'd keep the template shop going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade change your personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe settle down. I've been putting off living with my girlfriend, Jo, because I like having my own space and my own rent. With ten years of runway, that probably happens in the next couple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself when the robots arrive in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to be the person running the AI for twenty car dealers. And if that goes too, by 2039 I'd want enough saved to retrain without panic. I don't think anyone's safe by then, but ten years is enough to get ready.

say: This is the version where we **actually get to plan**, so plan.
Everyone should **start a side business** now while there's time.
think: Ten years is long enough to **build something real** before the design job goes.
By **37** I'd hope to run a small business that owns its clients.
do: Stay at Tallyho **two or three years** and get the production lead role.
Go solo running **dealers' ads with AI** for a monthly fee.
Invest monthly in a simple **index fund** and keep the template shop.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine, with room to breathe.
S4.quote: The graphic design job still goes in ten years, but I'd have moved before it did.
fieldNote: The decade makes him **optimistic**: he sees time to build a business before the job ends.
He'd finally **move in** with his girlfriend Jo, a choice he'd delayed.
Still honest that **nobody is safe** once robots arrive in 2039.

steps.text: Put a fixed sum into an index fund each month
Leave Tallyho after three years to run dealers' ads solo
Move in with Jo within the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my whole value is being early, and in that one being early only buys me about a year. What would help is a cheap, fast way to learn a hands-on trade, like short paid courses in signage or wrapping, and clear rules so small agencies can't be undercut overnight by the platforms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who ends up owning the tools. People like me can set up the AI tools, but I'm renting them from somebody huge. If the people at the top own everything, being early doesn't count for much.

headlineQuote: People like me can set up the AI tools, but I'm renting them from somebody huge. If the people at the top own everything, being early doesn't count for much.
portrait: Ben is a 27-year-old designer at **Tallyho Media**, making ads for car dealers, gyms and garden centres.
He uses AI **every day** and is the agency's go-to person for new tools.
He has about **three months** saved, lives alone, and sells ad templates on the side.
In the AGI versions he races to **own something**, a client list or a business share, before design wages vanish.
Calm in the mild worlds, he's **alarmed by 2028** because his early-adopter edge lasts only a year.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being early with the tools only buys him about a year.
whatWouldHelp: Short, paid courses in a **hands-on trade** like signage or wrapping.
Rules so platforms can't **undercut small agencies** overnight.
